turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Sure. Sounds good. I guess since we're on the topic of category creating versus not category creating, I'll start with an example that's very relevant to that. So we worked with RAMP in their very early days, and one of their first product announcements that we did together was the launch of their bill pay offering. And so at the time, I think they were like a three billion dollar company, something along those lines. So big, but not as big as they are today. Product news rarely gets big feature coverage, especially for something along the lines of a bill pay offering for B2B companies. (00:45:09): And so essentially the way that we framed the story was how RAMP was now able to take on Bill.com, which at the time I'm not sure if it still is, was one of the best performing FinTech IPOs public company that really had still only captured two percent of this market overall. And so by positioning it as allowing them to take on this massive incumbent that was getting a lot of press, we actually were able to get a CNBC story on the launch of this product. Generally they won't even consider product stories, but they really liked the angle of this underdog doing something that could take on a piece of market share from them. (00:45:47): And the next day there was actually another story about how Bill.com stock had gone down and they did make mention of RAMP's news in that story. So it ended up really just, it was a very powerful way of telling the narrative there. (00:46:02): And another way, if we hadn't pitched it like that would've just been RAMP brings simple, seamless, streamlined ability to do vendor payments and new finance offering, first of its kind. All these things that might be how you would talk in your customer emails, but if I had pitched it that way, probably wouldn't have been a story. So if we had pitched it as them creating a new category of this all in one software, which I mean, yeah, it could be argued, that's another way to tell the story. I don't think CNBC would've been interested.
turns.zh:
好的。听起来不错。既然我们正在讨论创建品类与不创建品类的话题，我想先举个与此非常相关的例子。我们在RAMP初创阶段就与他们合作，共同推出了他们的账单支付服务。这时候，他们的公司估值约30亿美元，虽然规模不算小，但远不及如今的规模。产品新闻通常很难获得大篇幅报道，尤其是针对B2B公司账单支付这类产品。（00:45:09）我们当时的宣传策略是突出RAMP如何挑战Bill.com。Bill.com当时（不确定现在是否还是如此）是表现最出色的金融科技上市公司之一，但其市场份额仅占2%。通过将RAMP定位为挑战这个备受关注的行业巨头，我们成功地让CNBC报道了这款产品的发布。通常CNBC不会考虑产品新闻，但他们很欣赏RAMP作为挑战者有机会从巨头手中抢占市场份额的叙事角度。（00:45:47）次日，又有报道称Bill.com股价下跌，文中还提到了RAMP的新闻。这次宣传策略堪称巧妙。

如果我们没有这样包装，宣传重点可能只是RAMP带来了简单、无缝、流畅的供应商支付功能，以及首创的金融产品。但那样的话，可能根本不会成为新闻。如果我们将其定位为RAMP开创了全能型软件的新品类，虽然也可以这么说，但CNBC大概不会感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: So, okay, another example, we work with a company called Column Tax, which is embedded tax filing software. So essentially they work with other FinTech's to allow people to file their taxes within the tools that they already use. And last year they partnered with a company called Propel that offers SNAP benefits. So essentially for low income families to receive the government benefits to offer tax filing directly within the app that they've created. (00:47:04): And that was one thing that they were doing amidst many other customers, that they had lots of different threads we could pull on with them, but we decided to really just focus our press strategy on that one initiative because it allowed us to tell macro story about TurboTax had to pay all these fines for practices that many considered unsavory around calling themselves free but not really being free. The IRS is building a free filing system, but it's in its very early days. (00:47:35): So the fact that they were having this offering that was supporting a lot of low income families, and I believe 40% of the people that filed their taxes with Column hadn't filed taxes in the previous year, so hadn't gotten a return. It's like identifying the piece of the story that's most interesting and then doubling down on that. So we were able to get a great fast company piece instead of pitching this macro here are Column Tax's latest growth metrics, and they're announcing a partnership with Propel. And so it's like...
turns.zh: 好的，再举个例子。我们与一家名为Column Tax的公司合作，他们开发的是嵌入式报税软件。基本上，他们与其他金融科技公司合作，让用户能在已有的工具中完成报税。去年，他们与提供SNAP福利的Propel公司达成合作，帮助低收入家庭直接在Propel开发的应用内领取政府福利并完成报税。（00:47:04）：这只是他们众多合作项目中的一项。我们本可以深入挖掘与其他客户的合作案例，但最终决定将宣传重点聚焦于这项举措，因为它能让我们讲述TurboTax的宏观故事——该公司因标榜“免费”实则收费的做法被处以巨额罚款，而美国国税局目前正在开发免费报税系统，但尚处于早期阶段。（00:47:35）：Column Tax的这项服务惠及了大量低收入家庭。据统计，使用Column Tax报税的用户中，有40%的人前一年未曾报税。这就需要找到最引人注目的故事点，并深挖其内涵。比如，我们没有简单罗列TurboTax的宏观增长数据，而是通过这项与Propel的合作案例，突出其为低收入家庭提供帮助的价值。这样既能吸引读者，又能精准传达TurboTax的核心主张。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Growth metrics, and they're announcing a partnership with Propeller. And so it's figuring out how to tie it to these things that people actually care about, and not just the company's messaging I think is our job.
turns.zh: 增长数据，以及他们宣布与Propel合作的消息。关键在于要将这些信息与人们真正关心的内容相结合，而不仅仅是公司层面的宣传，这才是我们的职责所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, is there any other examples? Otherwise, I'll share your pitch of someone coming on my podcast, and what worked about that.
turns.zh: 太棒了，还有其他案例吗？如果没有的话，我会分享你提到的让某位嘉宾上播客的案例，以及其中的成功之处。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I do want to share one more, because it's my favorite. I want to share my favorite funding story that I worked on. And so I'm actually going to pull it up, because this one is very graphic, in terms of how we went about showing the product. So we worked with a company called Gamma, which is essentially bringing a PowerPoint into something that's much more modern, and interactive, and usable. So when we did their launch, they were a seed stage company, we tried to get really creative with how we could display or talk about the company. And so instead of doing your standard company blog posts, we actually made a Gamma presentation, and we kind of included all these fun elements that made it really interesting to reporters. So firstly, it's a visual platform. So we created... Or actually I don't want to take credit for this. The Gamma team created this great visual. (00:49:11): And we kept it very to the point. Every year, half a billion people create presentations in Google Slides and PowerPoint. We're not using marketing language here, we're talking in a very direct way, we're including fund visuals. We talk about Gamma's mission, pretty short, this is not a long essay on why the company exists. And then we include some customer love, so they're early stage, so we didn't really have necessarily growth metrics that we wanted to share. So we tried to make it a little bit more personal, and focus on actual users and what they're saying, while also showing the product capability here. And then instead of doing a long thing on each investor, we just bulleted who the investors are, which is very to the point, easy for a reporter to repurpose. (00:49:55): And then the fun part that I really loved, is we did a video from the lead investor talking about why she invested, instead of including an investor quote. So it's a little bit different than what you expect. And their videos are fun, because they have all these interactive elements. And yeah, team photo, make it a little more personal. And that was about it. But anyways, it was a very successful story, and I believe the title of the TechCrunch article that we got as a result was Gamma Brings PowerPoint into the 21st Century. Exactly, that's exactly what we're talking. Maybe they are creating a new category, we weren't talking about it then, we're talking about how it's better than the existing solutions. And so yeah, I guess the piece of advice there, is feel free to get kind of fun and creative with it, and don't just follow the typical issuing press release format.
turns.zh:
我还想再分享一个案例，因为这是我最喜欢的。我想分享我参与过的最喜欢的融资故事。实际上，我现在要把它调出来，因为这个案例在展示产品方面做得很生动。我们与一家名为Gamma的公司合作，他们本质上是将PowerPoint升级为更现代、更具互动性和实用性的平台。当时我们为他们做推广时，他们还处于种子阶段。我们试图以创新方式展示或介绍这家公司。因此，我们没有采用标准的公司博客文章，而是制作了一个Gamma演示文稿，并加入了许多趣味元素，让记者们觉得很有意思。首先，这是一个视觉平台。我们创建了……其实这不是我的功劳——Gamma团队设计了这个很棒的视觉效果。我们保持了简洁明了。每年，有5亿人在Google Slides和PowerPoint上制作演示文稿。我们没有使用营销术语，而是用非常直接的方式讲述，加入了融资视觉图。我们简短地讲述了Gamma的使命——这不是一篇长篇大论，解释公司存在的意义。然后，我们加入了客户好评，因为他们处于早期阶段，所以没有太多可以分享的增长数据。因此，我们试图让内容更具个人色彩，聚焦实际用户及其反馈，同时展示产品功能。相较于对每位投资者进行长篇介绍，我们只用项目符号列出投资者名单，既简洁又便于记者转载。（00:49:55）  
最有趣的部分是，我们没有采用投资者引语，而是让首席投资者拍摄视频，讲述她投资的原因。这与人们的预期不同。他们的视频很有趣，充满互动元素。还有团队照片，让内容更具个人色彩。总之，这个案例非常成功。结果TechCrunch的文章标题是《Gamma将PowerPoint带入21世纪》。没错，这正是我们所谈论的。也许他们正在开创一个新类别，但当时我们没有提及这一点，而是强调它比现有解决方案更出色。所以，我想给出的建议是，尽可能让内容有趣且富有创意，不要局限于传统的新闻稿格式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is that something we could link to for people to check out? Is that just on their site?
turns.zh: 那我们能给用户提供链接让他们查看吗？还是说这只在他们的网站上？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 可以的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, I actually had to for some reason do some digging to get it. But yeah, I have it now, so I can give it to you.
turns.zh: 是啊，因为某些原因我确实费了些功夫才找到它。不过现在我终于拿到了，可以交给你了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. And the way that you use that is when you sent emails or DMs to reporters, you included this link?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。那你使用这个方法的方式是，在给记者发邮件或私信时，会附上这个链接吗？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: After they had that they're potentially interested, because again, if I had shared it right off the bat, it would be their prerogative to just publish it essentially or share it publicly. And I guess one important note, is everything you say to a reporter in an email is on the record, and so that's why I make the point on not sharing the entire story right off the bat.
turns.zh: 等他们拿到链接后，如果他们感兴趣的话，因为如果我一开始就把整个故事分享出去，他们完全可以直接发布或公开分享。我觉得有一点很重要的是，你在邮件里对记者说的一切都会被记录下来，所以这就是为什么我不建议一开始就分享整个故事的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So many companies won't have... They're not a deck product, so they can't do something like this. But the takeaways for other folks here, is be just very human in the language, the investors are just bullet points, make it fun, add some visuals, don't just have blurbs, and paragraphs, and things like that.
turns.zh: 明白了。很多公司没有……他们不是甲方产品，所以没法做这种事。但对在座的其他人来说，关键是要让语言更人性化，投资者只是要点，要让内容有趣，加入一些视觉效果，别只有段落和摘要之类的。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. I think reporters are used to getting the same thing all the time, and so this one obviously worked well for the format. But I think we try to always think of, what can we do that's slightly different for this one? Or how can we make this a little more fun? I guess the one exception, if the product is very technical, and you have a very technical audience, and you're probably going to work with a very technical reporter, it's totally fine to talk to your audience in those cases, and you don't need to necessarily dumb it down so everyone can understand. But that doesn't mean... I mean, you can do that while still using clear and concise language.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得记者已经习惯了收到千篇一律的材料，所以这次的格式显然很成功。但我认为我们应该总是思考，能为这次活动做些稍微不同的尝试？或者如何让它更有趣一点？我觉得唯一的例外情况是，如果产品非常技术性，而且你的受众也是技术型的，你可能会和一个技术型记者合作，那完全没问题，可以用技术术语和他们交流，不必为了让所有人都能理解而简化术语。但这并不意味着……我的意思是，你可以做到这一点同时保持语言清晰简洁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let me share the element of the pitch that you sent me, that convinced me to bring this guest on. So this is going to be the chief product officer at NewBank. I barely know anything about NewBank. And so in your email to me, you basically had just two bullet points, and the way you put is, "Two fun facts about NewBank, growth has been 80 to 90% organic because of the way they try to make customers fanatical about the product." And to me that's like, "Wow, that's very rare, is 80, 90% of your growth being organic." So to me is like, "That's an interesting story." And then the other tidbit is, "NewBank is bigger than Coinbase, Robinhood, Affirm, SoFi, and Lemonade combined. Seriously, so much bigger than people in the US realize." Which I 100% did not realize. So to me both were just like, "Okay, this is an interesting story to tell, I think people would be very curious to hear how a company like this operates." So now I'm going to start getting all these emails from people, all these couple bullet points.
turns.zh: 好的，我来分享一下你发给我的推销材料中的亮点，让我决定邀请这位嘉宾。接下来要介绍的是NewBank的首席产品官。我对NewBank几乎一无所知。所以你在发给我的邮件里只有两个要点，你是这样写的：“关于NewBank的两个趣闻：由于他们致力于让客户对产品着迷，80%到90%的增长都是自然增长。” 这让我觉得“哇，80%、90%的增长都是自然增长，这太罕见了。” 所以我觉得“这真是个有趣的故事。” 另一个亮点是：“NewBank的规模比Coinbase、Robinhood、Affirm、SoFi和Lemonade加起来还要大得多。说真的，美国人对它的规模远远低估了。” 我完全不知道这个情况。所以对我来说，这两个亮点都让我觉得“好吧，这是一个值得讲述的有趣故事，我觉得人们会很好奇这样一家公司是如何运作的。” 现在我要开始收到人们发来的邮件，里面都是这几个要点了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: They're going to combine a bunch of companies, and see which they're bigger than.
turns.zh: 他们打算合并多家公司，然后看看哪家公司规模更大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, or use AI to help them figure this out. But I think what you identified here is just what I get excited about. Is there any advice there of just what you did there that other people can learn from?
turns.zh: 是啊，或者用人工智能来帮他们弄清楚。但我觉得你在这里提到的正是让我兴奋的地方。有什么建议吗？比如你刚才做的那些事，别人能从中学到什么？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think with pitching you, speaking to the audience, it's not just about having... You don't want the most well-known CEOs all the time, you're not looking just for the biggest companies and the most well-known people. You're looking for the things that they can talk about, and how the things that they can talk about are relevant to your audience. And with the first bullet, it was indexing on that. The second bullet was more so like, "Hey, you might not know about this company." And it's a little bit of a unique one, I wouldn't necessarily always include that. But to me the first bullet was really what mattered, because it wasn't just about the fact that they were a huge company, it's that they grew in a unique way, and I knew that was the kind of thing that you'd be interested in.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，在向听众推销产品时，关键不在于拥有……你不想总是请来最知名的CEO，也不是只找最大型的公司和最有名的人物。你要关注的是他们能谈论的内容，以及这些内容与听众的相关性。第一个要点就是围绕这一点展开的。第二个要点更多的是说，“嘿，你可能对这家公司不熟悉。”这是一家比较独特的公司，我不一定会每次都提到它。但对我来说，第一个要点才是真正重要的，因为关键不在于他们是一家大公司，而在于他们以独特的方式实现了增长，而我知道这正是你感兴趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how did you figure that out? Is it from emails we were exchanging ahead of that? Is it listening to some podcasts? How did you get to those conclusions?
turns.zh: 那你是怎么想到这一点的？是通过我们之前交流的邮件吗？还是听了一些播客？你是怎么得出这些结论的？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, listening certainly helps. But I do think just figuring out... If you even just scrolled the names of all the episodes that you've done, it would be pretty easy to spot a trend there. And so you're not talking about product launches, you are not talking about entrepreneurial journeys, you're talking about tactical lessons. And so pitching people based on those sort of things, I don't even think you necessarily need to listen to a whole bunch of episodes most of the time, maybe occasionally you want to gut check something before you reach out. But yeah, you can tell a lot just by doing a little bit of research. (00:54:53): And then we did have a little back and forth, because I will take responsibility, I did try pitching you on a CEO at one point, which I know you don't have on as guests.
turns.zh: 是的，倾听当然有帮助。但我确实认为只要能弄清楚……如果你甚至只是浏览一下你做过的所有播客的标题，就能很容易发现其中的趋势。你不会谈论产品发布，也不会谈论创业历程，而是谈论策略性的经验教训。所以基于这些内容来推销，我甚至认为大多数时候你不必听太多播客，也许偶尔在联系对方之前需要确认一下。但是，只要做一点研究，你就能了解很多情况了。（00:54:53）：然后我们还讨论了一下，我得承认，我确实有过一次尝试向你推销一位CEO，但我知道你从不邀请CEO作为嘉宾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Once in a while, very rarely.
turns.zh: 偶尔，非常罕见。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, actually, there's obviously some exceptions. But I had known the subject matter you were looking for, but I did not spot the trend that you've never had CEOs on. So I think my pitch was actually okay, but the spokesperson was not the kind of person that you would want on. So maybe you won't get it right 100% of the time, but you can tell a lot just by doing some searches.
turns.zh: 是的，显然也有例外。但我确实了解你寻找的主题，但我没有发现你从未邀请过CEO参加节目这个趋势。所以我觉得我的推销其实还不错，但那位发言人并不是你希望邀请的那种人。所以也许你不会每次都百分之百成功，但只要做一些搜索，你就能了解很多情况了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And oftentimes I just reply, "Here's my policy." And then, "Okay, good to know." Kind of along these lines, something I wanted to ask earlier, you mentioned a few publications to go after, and then how to pitch people. Obviously the way that you're describing takes a bunch of time. How many people are you often emailing, DMing per attempt to get a story? Because it sounds like it's not a ton, and so you have time to do these sorts of custom pitches. Or is it a lot higher than it sounds?
turns.zh: 很多时候我只会回复：“这是我的报道方针。” 然后再说：“好的，知道了。” 大致就是这样。之前我想问的是，你提到了几家可以联系的媒体，还有如何向对方推销你的故事。显然你描述的方式需要耗费大量时间。你每次尝试获取报道时，平均会给多少人发邮件或发私信？因为听起来发送量并不大，所以你才有时间进行这种个性化推销。或者实际发送量比听起来要多得多？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I would say for hard news, funding, the startup launch, those sort of things, less, and I try to really stagger it because we're offering exclusives, and I highly recommend offering exclusives. So the worst thing that can happen is two reporters reply, and are both interested, and you have to go back to one and say, "Nevermind." And sometimes that's okay if they left you, if it's been a week or something, they hadn't gotten back, and they'll understand. So it's fine to move on without getting an answer. So I would say, yeah, with the funding story, it could be anywhere from one to six reporters on average, sometimes more. With stuff like general just outreach, relationship building, trying to get on podcasts, it kind of is a numbers game, and you really have to balance quality and quantity. (00:56:38): And that's why I love starting with the first note and not saying much, and just saying, "Hey, you open to guest ideas?" Because it allows you to do more. I'd rather do that than send a bad pitch, and not have it be targeted to the right sort of audience. And so that's kind of a way to play the numbers game while still being respectful. But yeah, I mean, with some clients maybe they get one opportunity for every 20 or 30 things that we send. And so yeah, we try not to do... We don't do blasting media, it's not about sending the same pitch to a single list of people. It's figuring out, which ones do I want to really double down on because they're the perfect target? And you'll keep trying, you'll be really custom, which deserve maybe a slightly higher level note, which deserve a DM, and just figuring out your strategy from that.
turns.zh: 我会说对于硬新闻、融资、创业公司启动这类内容，发送量较少。我会尽量分批次发送，因为我们提供独家报道，而且我强烈建议提供独家报道。最糟糕的情况是两个记者回复，都感兴趣，但你不得不退一步跟其中一个说：“算了。” 有时候如果他们一周内没回复，也没关系，他们会理解的。所以没得到回复也可以继续下一个目标。就融资报道而言，平均可能有1到6个记者感兴趣，有时更多。对于一般性的外联、关系建立、尝试上播客之类的，这就是个数字游戏，你必须平衡质量和数量。（00:56:38）这就是为什么我喜欢从第一封邮件开始，不说太多，只是问：“嘿，你对嘉宾提案感兴趣吗？” 这样能有更多发挥空间。比起发送不针对目标受众的糟糕推销，我更愿意这样做。这也是在尊重对方的前提下玩数字游戏的方法。但确实，有些客户可能20到30次发送才有一次机会。所以我们尽量避免群发邮件，不是在给单一的媒体列表发送相同的推销内容。而是分析哪些媒体是完美目标，值得重点投入。不断尝试，针对不同媒体采用不同的策略，比如有些值得发送更高级别的邮件，有些则适合发送私信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay. Do you have examples of pitches, announcements that were not as effective as they could have been, and advice for how they could have been better?
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。你能举些推销效果不佳的例子吗？还有如何改进呢？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, I have some excerpts that I pulled from press releases where I think there's room for improvement. So Lenny, I want to read one to you, and then I want to see if you can tell me what this company does. Okay, "Today X announced their workflow automation product, which combines AI assistance, human in the loop collaboration, and a robust multiplayer experience to help teams save time."
turns.zh: 是的，我从新闻稿中提取了一些片段，我觉得有些地方可以改进。那么，Lenny，我想先读一段给你听听，然后看看你能不能说出这家公司的业务内容。好的，"X公司今天宣布推出其工作流自动化产品，该产品结合了AI辅助、人机协作以及强大的多人协作体验，助力团队节省时间。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely no idea what's going on.
turns.zh: 完全不知道这是怎么回事。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: You kind of gained something from workflow automation, and then after that it's like, "Wait, what?"
turns.zh: 你好像从工作流自动化中获得了一些好处，但之后就有点困惑了："等等，什么情况？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a bunch of things.
turns.zh: 就是一堆乱七八糟的东西。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Okay, now let me read to an excerpt from the TechCrunch article, and this is how TechCrunch positioned it, "A new automation startup is setting out to eat Zapier's lunch. It helps people tackle mundane and repetitive tasks, and goes beyond the triggers and actions popularized by similar platforms like Zapier." So to me, yeah, it's a better version of Zapier, where they aren't just doing triggers and actions, and there's a little more substance and depth to it. If you know what Zapier is, you can kind of start to figure out what they do based on that.
turns.zh: 好的，我现在要读一段TechCrunch文章的节选。TechCrunch是这么定位的："一家新兴的自动化初创公司正试图挑战Zapier的市场地位。它帮助人们处理重复性的日常任务，超越了Zapier等类似平台流行的触发器和动作模式。" 在我看来，没错，它就是一个更优化的Zapier版本，不只是触发器和动作，还有更丰富的内涵和深度。只要你了解Zapier，就能大致理解他们的业务方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it comes back to your point about referencing incumbent to help you understand what the heck you're talking about
turns.zh: 是啊，这又回到了你提到的，通过引用现有公司来帮助读者理解你在说什么。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: And you wouldn't necessarily need to do that in your press release, but I think they could have been a lot clearer, and not use... Because terms like robust multiplayer experience, that makes it sound like a game. Are we talking about just collaborative multiple users? Human in the loop collaboration, isn't all collaboration between humans, and we're all in the loop? AI assistance, that just means they use AI. So yeah, sometimes I push my clients to like, "Okay, let's talk through what each of these phrases actually means. And if you can't articulate it, then let's change it to the way that you just articulated it, and it might be more successful." So yeah, that's a good way to do it. And just read it out loud, read it out loud and see if someone understands it.
turns.zh: 但你不一定需要在新闻稿中这样做，但我觉得他们本可以更清晰明了，不必用那些术语。比如"robust multiplayer experience"，听起来像个游戏。我们说的难道不是多人协作吗？"human in the loop collaboration"，不就是人与人之间的协作吗？我们不都是参与其中吗？AI assistance，就是说他们用了AI。是啊，有时候我会提醒客户："好吧，让我们仔细拆解一下每个术语的含义。如果你无法清晰表达，那就改成你刚刚解释的那样，可能更容易理解。" 这确实是个好方法。大声读出来，看看有没有人能听懂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone hearing this is like, "How could possibly anybody think that was great? How did these come about, these really bad descriptions?" I know it's hard to come up with something really short and pithy, but where do these come from?
turns.zh: 听到这些的人可能会说："怎么会有人觉得这写得好呢？这些描述怎么能这么糟糕？" 我知道要写出简洁明了的文案很难，但这些描述到底从何而来？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: It's just a culture within marketing and comms, of this is how we're supposed to write. And I just think that's a majority of how people do it, and they think it sounds smart, or they think it sounds more professional. I just think it's just how people are trained. And so even when we bring on someone new, part of my job is stripping away at a lot of that, and getting people... Everyone's capable of talking like a human being, we do it every day. But it's stripping away that thing that goes off in your head that you're supposed to be writing in a very marketingy way. Because I would say at least 50% of releases are like that, it's not a small problem.
turns.zh: 这不过是营销和公关领域的一种文化规范，仿佛这就是我们应该写作的方式。我觉得大多数人都是这样做的，他们认为这样听起来更聪明、更专业。我觉得这不过是人们被训练出来的习惯。即使我们招募新人，我的部分工作就是要消除这种习惯，让人们……每个人都能像正常人一样说话，我们每天都在这么做。但关键是，要消除那种在你脑海中浮现的“必须用营销术语写作”的想法。因为我敢说，至少50%的新闻稿都是这样的，这绝不是个小问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. I love the advice you shared of just trying to say it out loud, hearing yourself, what does it sound like? Do you have any other tips for trying to make it something people get and connect to? I know that, again, it takes a lot of time to really do well and it's very context specific, but is there any other tricks that you find help you communicate what you're actually offering?
turns.zh: 好的。我很欣赏你提到的那个建议，就是大声把想法说出来，听听自己说出来的效果如何？你还有其他帮助人们理解并产生共鸣的技巧吗？我知道，要做好这件事需要花很多时间，而且因环境而异，但你有没有什么其他技巧可以帮助传达你实际提供的东西？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: It's talking through the basic questions, what does this product do? Who is it for? Who are your customers? If you can answer each of those in one sentence... What product launch are we talking about here? If you can just answer each of those verbally, chances are you're not going to be far away from what you're looking for. Because when I talk to marketers, and founders, and teams, generally in the conversations I have no trouble understanding what they're talking about. They can articulate it just fine, it's only in the writing that it gets that way. So actually I think it's kind of easier to solve than many might realize. And then also I think there is some skill involved in removing words, not over explaining, you can make things more concise. But at the bare minimum, just strip out all the jargon, that's the first step.
turns.zh: 就是把基本问题过一遍，这个产品有什么功能？面向谁？客户是谁？如果你能用一句话回答每个问题……我们现在谈论的是哪次产品发布？如果你能口头回答这些问题，那你离你想要的结果应该不远了。因为当我和营销人员、创始人以及团队交流时，通常我能理解他们在说什么。他们能清晰地表达自己的想法，但写作时却不行。所以我觉得这个问题比很多人想象的要容易解决得多。此外，我认为去除冗余词汇、避免过度解释也是一项技能，你可以让内容更简洁。但最起码，先去掉所有行话，这是第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. So one way to think about it is, just think about, what does it do? Who is it for? Who are the customers? Is there something else along those lines that you shared there as a bullet point?
turns.zh: 我很赞同。那么思考一下：它有什么功能？面向谁？客户是谁？你有没有其他类似的要点可以分享？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Well, I mean, if you're talking about what makes this business interesting? Why should people care? And not over indexing on that. I think that's just one part of the overall story, is why people should care about this business. And then what's new? Is it growth metrics? Is it the customer piece? Is it product? What makes this timely and relevant right now?
turns.zh: 嗯，我的意思是，如果你要谈论这个业务的亮点是什么？为什么人们应该关注它？别过度强调这一点。我认为这只是整体故事的一部分，说明人们为什么应该关注这个业务。然后还有什么？是增长数据？还是客户部分？还是产品？是什么让它在当下既及时又相关？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. There's actually this awesome Twitter thread from a couple of days ago, where the CEO of Product Hunt did this thread where he asked people, "Share your tagline, and I will give you a much better version of the tagline." And he's really good at this. So I'm going to link to it in the show notes, where he can give you an example of what it looks like from bad to good.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。几天前推特上有个超棒的讨论，Product Hunt的CEO发起了一个话题，问大家：“分享你们的宣传语，我会给你们一个更好的版本。” 他在这方面真的很在行。我会在节目笔记里附上链接，他会给你们展示从糟糕到优秀的例子。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I love that. That's exactly the kind of thing I would love to do too, because it's so fun and so easy.
turns.zh: 我超爱这个主意。这正是我也想做的事情，因为既有趣又简单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's easy if you're good at it, most people are not great at it. You mentioned press release in this example, you shared thoughts on value of press release, traditional press release versus not.
turns.zh: 如果你擅长这个的话确实不难，但大多数人都不擅长。刚才你提到新闻稿这个例子，你分享了对新闻稿价值的看法，以及传统新闻稿和非传统新闻稿的区别。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Press releases came about because reporters would be checking news wires for ideas of what stories they want to write. No reporters do that anymore, or a very small percentage, I don't know any reporters that do that anymore. So now it's this thing where you go to one of the PR distribution services, you pay them anywhere between 300 to $2,000, that's literally what it costs, and they put it on the wire. And for the more expensive services, it does get syndicated to this press release section of some business websites. No one, in my opinion, goes there for their news. I've personally never read an article, like a Yahoo Finance article, that was a press release syndication. So in that sense, they are not helpful for getting eyeballs. They also require... Going back to that more marketing form of writing, they require that you write like that. (01:03:39): The standard press release format, it's so formulaic, and I think it actually encourages that more marketing speak. The benefit is that you're getting all the news details in one place, so it's relevant for a reporter. However, you can do the exact same thing in a blog post. And the blog post can be this first person piece of content that's written by either the founder, or the product lead, or whatever executive, that has a lot more flexibility in the style. You can kind of write it however you want, it can still include all the same news elements. And it's much more shareable on social, you're not going to share a link to a press release on your Twitter or on your LinkedIn, but a blog, for sure. You can add your own graphics, it's great. (01:04:21): And you're also encouraging people to go to something that lives on your website versus this black hole of a newsletter. I should be fair, so I think that the reason that people say that they still do them, is that it helps with SEO. However, I've read a few articles that have said that Google no longer does prioritize press releases in SEO, so I don't know how much that holds up. And that it signals to the market that the company is more serious, so that's a perception thing. I personally think that blogs actually signal a more modern, kind of cool company than a press release. But at a certain stage in your growth, public companies, they do press releases for earnings, makes 100% sense. There are certain rules around when companies do need to issue press releases, so there's still a use case for them, I just think your average early to mid-stage startup doesn't need them.
turns.zh: 新闻稿的诞生源于记者们会浏览新闻通讯线路，以寻找可报道的素材。如今，很少有记者会这样做了，或者说比例极低。我不知道还有哪位记者还在这么做。所以现在的情况是，你去找某个公关分发服务平台，支付300到2000美元不等的费用（这就是实际花费），他们就会把新闻稿发布到通讯线路上。对于更贵的服务，它们确实会把新闻稿分发到一些商业网站的专属新闻发布区。但在我看来，没人会去那里获取新闻。我个人从未读过雅虎财经等网站上由新闻稿分发服务生成的文章。因此，从获取流量的角度来看，这些新闻稿没什么用。它们还需要……回到那种更具营销性的写作风格，你必须按照他们的要求来写。（01:03:39）标准的新闻稿格式太程式化了，我认为这反而助长了营销化表达的风气。好处是记者能在一处获取所有新闻细节，但你完全可以在博客文章中做到同样的效果。博客文章可以由创始人、产品负责人或其他高管撰写，这种第一人称的叙事方式在风格上灵活得多。你可以随心所欲地写作，同样能包含所有新闻要素。而且在社交媒体上更容易传播——你肯定不会在推特或领英上分享新闻稿链接，但博客文章肯定可以。你还能添加自己的图片，效果很棒。（01:04:21）你还能鼓励人们访问公司官网，而不是把注意力集中在那些形同黑洞的邮件通讯上。我得说实话，那些坚持使用新闻稿的人，是因为它们有助于提升SEO排名。不过我读过一些文章称，谷歌已不再在SEO中优先考虑新闻稿，所以这点存疑。新闻稿还能向市场传递公司更专业、更靠谱的形象，但这只是个心理暗示。我个人认为博客能更好地展现公司现代、酷炫的一面。不过在公司发展到一定阶段后，上市公司确实需要发布财报新闻稿，这完全说得通。公司确实有特定规则规定何时必须发布新闻稿，所以新闻稿仍有其存在的意义，但我认为普通初创企业或中期阶段的公司根本不需要它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This mention of blogs is where I wanted to go next actually, so it's a good segue. But before we do that, is there any other examples that you wanted to share of less than ideal ways of pitching a product?
turns.zh: 关于博客的讨论正是我接下来想谈的，这是一个很好的过渡话题。但在讨论之前，你是否还有其他不理想的产品推广案例想分享？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: One sentence I found in a press release that a lot of companies want to include that I always try to remove is... Well here, I'll give you the sentence, "Since exiting stealth in May, we've witnessed a 700% increase in organizations using our product." You're saying that since you were in stealth to now you saw a 700% increase, so you could have had one customer, now you have seven. And it's every company wants to do these percentage growth stats when they just launched, and I've never seen reporters include that in their stories. (01:05:50): And so there are ways to give signals of how fast you're growing without being that kind of disingenuous. One way that you could put something similar is, "Our revenue hit six figures at the end of last year, and has been growing about 30% each quarter, with 40% of adoption coming from the enterprise sector." So you're giving color to the growth, and you can kind of play with that, it doesn't need to be exactly something like that. But if you can make it a little more specific, I'm not against doing percentages, but I think there's a way to balance that with something that seems a little more realistic.
turns.zh: 有一句话我曾在新闻稿中发现，很多公司都想加入其中，但我总会努力删掉它……好吧，我给你们看这句话：“自五月份结束隐身模式以来，我们见证了使用我们产品的组织数量增长了700%。” 你说的是从隐身模式结束到现在，用户量增长了700%，所以可能之前只有一个客户，现在有七个了。每个公司在刚推出产品时都喜欢抛出这种百分比增长数据，但我从未见过记者在报道中采用这种说法。（01:05:50）其实有办法传达增长速度又不显得虚假。比如，“去年年底我们的营收突破六位数，之后每个季度增长约30%，其中40%的客户来自企业级市场。” 这样既给出了增长细节，又可以灵活调整，不必完全照搬。但如果能更具体些，我不反对使用百分比数据，但要确保数据更贴近实际情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or, "We went from zero to six figures in ARR in X months."
turns.zh: 或者，“我们在X个月内营收从零增长到六位数。”

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, no, totally. And it doesn't need to be huge, especially if you're doing your first story, they're not expecting that you're necessarily going to have massive revenue. And so I think founders might sometimes be concerned that it's not going to seem big enough or significant enough, whereas from working with a lot of companies, it's kind of the case across the board.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。数据不必太夸张，尤其是初次报道时，记者不会期望你一开始就有巨额营收。所以我觉得创始人有时会担心数据不够吸引人或不够显著，但根据我的经验，这种情况普遍存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned a bunch of amazing companies, you've worked with Ramp, Perplexity, a few others. And people may feel like, of course you're getting pressed, those are amazing. Ramp grew to a 100 million AR in two years, Perplexity is this killer AI product, everyone's talking about AI. Most products are not that, they don't have as interesting of a story to tell. Is there either an example you could share of a company that didn't have an amazing story to tell, that you created an interesting story out of? Or just any advice for, how do you help find something that is a nugget that gets people excited?
turns.zh: 你提到了很多出色的公司，比如Ramp、Perplexity等。我知道人们会觉得这些公司备受关注，因为它们确实很棒。Ramp两年内营收就达到1亿美元，Perplexity是热门的AI产品，人人都谈论AI。但大多数公司并非如此，没有那么引人注目的故事。能否分享一个没有惊人故事的公司案例，通过巧妙包装让它变得有趣？或者有没有什么建议，如何挖掘能激发人们兴趣的亮点？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: So some of the examples I gave, so Clockwise and Column Tax aren't as big as some of the other brands I mentioned. So that's certainly actually the bulk of our business, I would say 80% of the companies we work with are at a stage where they haven't reached that kind of mass awareness yet. (01:07:40): Another really great company that we work with is Entropy. And so essentially they work with transaction data, they're an API. It's a very technical tool, it's not something that necessarily every reporter is going to instantly understand. But for them, we've actually really leaned into the founder story. She's this incredible woman who moved to the US, and actually struggled with getting her first apartment here because of the way that our credit scoring system is set up. And one of the use cases for what she's building actually directly relates to how our credit system could change in the future, and so we've been really leaning into that angle. And her personal story is really powerful. And so maybe sometimes the product isn't going to be something that you can easily pitch, but you can kind of find those other personal angles in or pull on certain threads.
turns.zh: 以上是我列举的几个例子，其中Clockwise和Column Tax的规模并不如我提到的其他一些品牌那么大。可以说，这确实是我们业务的主体部分——我们合作的80%公司目前尚未达到那种广泛认知的阶段。（01:07:40）：我们合作的另一家非常出色的公司是Entropy。他们主要处理交易数据，是一家API服务商。这是一款技术性很强的工具，并非每位记者都能一下子理解。但针对他们，我们着重讲述了创始人的故事。她是一位了不起的女性，移居美国后因信用评分体系的设置问题难以租到首套房。而她所开发的技术应用之一，直接关联到未来信用体系可能的变革方向，因此我们着重突出这一点。她的个人经历非常感人，也许有时产品本身难以推广，但你总能找到其他切入点或挖掘其中的情感价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there it connects back to find the publication that cares about these sorts of personal stories, because TechCrunch probably won't.
turns.zh: 这就需要找到对这类个人故事感兴趣的媒体平台，因为TechCrunch可能不感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. But she spoke at Money20/20, so it's useful for speaking abstracts too. Actually it was on a panel with Column Tax, we got them on together at Money20/20.
turns.zh: 是的。但她在Money20/20大会上发言了，所以这对演讲提案也很有帮助。实际上她和Column Tax同台出席了Money20/20的专题讨论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a win.
turns.zh: 真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: No, and we love doing that, it's so fun when you do have multiple companies that you can connect. Actually, that's kind of a good macro point as well. It doesn't always need to just be about you, if you have an idea for a conference session, reaching out to colleagues that you've worked with at other companies, peers, people that are building other things that maybe don't compete better in a similar space, and packaging that up as like, "Hey, this could be a really strong panel." It's actually way more successful than just pitching yourself.
turns.zh: 不，我们很乐意这样做。当你能把多家公司联系起来时，那种乐趣真是难以言表。说起来，这也是一个很好的宏观思考点：不必只关注自己。如果你对某个会议环节有想法，不妨联系在其他公司共事过的同事、同行，以及那些在相似领域但并非竞争对手的创业者，共同打磨出一个精彩的专题讨论。事实上，这样比单独推销自己要成功得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay. So you've mentioned a couple of times the rise of newsletters and podcasts. So there's kind of two buckets of questions here. One is going after these kind of non-traditional media platforms, and then the other is building your own following, and building a following on Twitter, for example. I know you worked closely with the CEO of Vox who's really good at this, and basically doesn't need press. Elon is amazing at this, maybe that's why he bought Twitter, he has this huge platform to talk about all the stuff. So maybe in the first bucket, talking about when you're trying to decide, should I go after traditional media, Vox, and VentureBeat, and Axios, and all these guys? Versus I'm going to go for newsletters. As an example, Ramp got a lot of benefit from Not Boring, that newsletter with Packy, who wrote about them constantly and loved it. And they're sponsored posts, and organic posts. So I guess the question there is just, how do you think about going after podcasts, newsletters, Twitter, LinkedIn, influencery platformy people versus traditional press?
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。你提到过几次新闻通讯和播客的兴起。所以这里有两个问题方向。一是如何利用这些非传统媒体平台，另一个是如何建立自己的粉丝群体，比如在Twitter上积累关注者。我知道你和Vox的CEO合作得很紧密，他在这方面很擅长，甚至不需要依赖传统媒体宣传。埃隆在这方面也很出色，也许这就是他收购Twitter的原因——他拥有一个巨大的平台来宣传所有内容。所以在第一个问题上，当你决定是去追逐传统媒体平台，比如Vox、VentureBeat、Axios等，还是选择新闻通讯时，该如何抉择？以Ramp为例，他们从Not Boring这样的新闻通讯中获益匪浅，Packy持续写作并大力推荐他们的产品，既有赞助内容，也有自然推广。所以问题在于，如何看待新闻通讯、播客、Twitter、LinkedIn、网红平台等与传统媒体的关系？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I think of newsletters and podcasts actually in the camp of, if we're pitching traditional press, we're 100% pitching those. Social is its own ball game, but I would not leave out newsletters and podcasts from any core PR strategy. To me, it's now just a part of any PR program that we're going to run, because it's just part of media now. And to me, it's just a very important part of media. In terms of social, I think doing social well is very hard. So you gave Aaron from Vox as an example, that was all 100% him. I think I helped with one tweet once about a Microsoft partnership that we did, and I was so excited.
turns.zh: 我认为新闻通讯和播客实际上属于PR策略的一部分。如果我们在推销传统媒体时，肯定会重点推广这些平台。社交媒体则另当别论，但我不认为PR核心策略应该排除新闻通讯和播客。对我来说，它们现在是任何PR项目的组成部分，因为它们已经成为媒体生态的重要组成部分，而且非常重要。至于社交媒体，我认为做好社交媒体推广非常困难。以Vox的Aaron为例，那完全是他的个人功劳。我记得我曾为微软与Vox的合作关系发过一条推文，当时我特别兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did it do?
turns.zh: 效果如何？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Actually really good. A publication ended up writing a story on the tweet about Microsoft and Vox partnership because of it. Yeah, so that was fun. But generally it's not always something that you can just turn on by hiring an agency. And I've seen many companies try doing that, and not necessarily see as much success as they'd hoped for. So if a founder is naturally good at that stuff, lean into it as much as humanly possible, go for it. If they're not, and you're trying to outsource it, it can be done to some success. But I don't necessarily think it's as easy as just posting three times a week on relevant topics, there has to be more going on there. I think that if the spokesperson or the executive that you're trying to build the presence of is willing to... Going back to what I said earlier, kind of push the limit.
turns.zh: 实际上效果很好。有一家媒体因为这条推文写了一篇关于微软与Vox合作的报道。是的，那很有趣。但通常这不是简单雇佣代理就能做到的。我见过很多公司尝试这样做，但效果不尽如人意。所以如果创始人天生擅长这类事务，那就尽可能多地投入精力；如果不擅长，又想外包出去，倒也能取得一定效果。但我不认为这就像每周在相关主题上发三条推文那么简单，背后必须有更多深层策略。比如，如果你想提升发言人或高管的曝光度，他们必须愿意突破常规，勇于尝试。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: ... Presence of is willing to, going back to what I said earlier, push the limit on opinions that they have, be bold, be controversial, then it could be worth potentially investing in. And I have seen it play out where reporters have seen those posts and used and quoted things in their articles as a result, so it can tie to your traditional media strategy a little bit, they're not necessarily fully siloed, but I would say if you're considering investing in social to just do corporate channels and not think about executives, you're really leaving a lot on the table. Corporate channels, it's very hard to build a following. (01:12:39): To get someone to follow a brand and care about a brand, you have to be bringing something new to the table, because they don't want to read your latest blog post, they don't want to read a relevant article that your social person just decided to put out there. When you have an executive, you're following a personality, you're following a person, ideally there's more flexibility with tone, all of that sort of stuff. And so I think it's important to think about it from the people perspective and not just the brand perspective.
turns.zh: ……正如我之前所说，如果有人愿意突破界限，勇于表达自己的观点，敢于引发争议，那么这种行为或许值得投入资源。我曾见过记者将此类帖子引用到文章中，这就能与传统媒体策略形成互补。两者并非完全割裂，但若你仅考虑投资企业官方账号，而忽视高管个人账号，那无疑是错失良机。企业账号很难积累粉丝群体。（01:12:39）要让用户关注并认可品牌，就必须提供新颖的内容——毕竟他们不愿阅读最新博客文章，也不感兴趣于社交团队随意发布的相关资讯。高管账号则不同，粉丝关注的是个性，关注的是人本身，理想情况下语气会更灵活多变。因此，必须从人的视角而非品牌视角来审视此事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to make it clear, the CEO or some execs should be the people tweeting and LinkedIn, and not the company as a brand?
turns.zh: 所以说清楚一点，CEO或其他高管应该亲自运营推特和领英账号，而非以公司品牌名义？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. And I don't know. I think that it can be a little industry specific as well for where it makes sense to be investing in the corporate channels. And you certainly can do that sort of thing. But I also think if you're going to do that, have an exec that you're also trying a social strategy with. Don't just do the plain corporate channels.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为在何种情况下投资企业官方账号可能因行业而异。你当然可以这么做，但我认为若要这么做，就应该让高管同时参与社交策略实践，而非仅局限于普通企业账号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I think of a brand doing this really well, it's Duolingo. They're just so hilarious and so ridiculous in there. And I don't know if the key is just funny is the way to go, and that's how you get any attention, but they're so funny and creative in their videos, especially TikTok.
turns.zh: 说到品牌在这方面做得非常出色的，我想到的是Duolingo。他们在平台上表现得既滑稽又夸张。我不确定是否只有搞笑才有关注度，但他们的视频确实非常有趣且富有创意，尤其是在TikTok上。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: It's interesting though, we're getting to the point where even brands having a personality on social is becoming its own meme. People are making fun of how all the fast food brands all are like these Gen Z like TikTok-
turns.zh: 不过有趣的是，我们正逐渐发现，品牌在社交媒体上展现个性本身也成为了一种文化现象。人们调侃所有快餐品牌都像Z世代那样活跃于TikTok——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they're all replying to each other on Twitter threads.
turns.zh: 甚至在推特话题中互相回复。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. And so things change quickly. So, yes, that was a good strategy, but you just have to stay on top of it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以情况变化很快。没错，这曾是个不错的策略，但你必须持续跟进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you talked about how if this comes naturally to you as a founder, obviously do it. I'm guessing for most people it doesn't. Do you find that it can work if you're just like, "I know this is important, I need to tweet often and share things," have you seen that work or is it just like it's just probably not going to be something that works great for you?
turns.zh: 嗯，你提到如果作为创始人这对你来说是自然而然的事情，那显然应该去做。但我猜对大多数人来说并非如此。你觉得如果只是强迫自己去发推文、分享内容，这样做能行得通吗？你见过这种方法有效过吗？还是说这对你来说可能效果不佳？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, I think it can work to some extent. Maybe you're not going to necessarily be going viral or getting hundreds or tens of thousands of followers. But for me personally I push myself to post on LinkedIn at least once a month, because every time I post we get at least one client inbound and maybe a candidate inbound. And so if you test it and you start to see value, push yourself to do it even if it doesn't come naturally. And that's, I guess, the nice thing about social is it's easy to test out. You can try doing it, you can post for a while, even for a month or two, see how it's going, and then adjust your strategy accordingly. (01:15:06): But, yes, I think for a lot of execs that we work with, it does feel like it's something that's really hard, there's a lot of overthinking, making sure it's right. You can get really in your head about it, and I totally understand that because I feel the same way. And so if it's taking up so much of your time and bandwidth just thinking about your social strategy, then I guess you can weigh if it makes sense to do that, but I think pushing yourself to try it is a great idea.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为在某种程度上还是能行得通的。也许你不会因此走红，收获数百或数千名粉丝。但就我个人而言，我会强迫自己每月至少在领英上发一次帖子，因为每次发帖至少能带来一个新客户或求职者的咨询。所以如果你尝试后发现确实有价值，就算不觉得自然也要坚持去做。这就是社交媒体的好处——你可以轻松测试效果。你可以尝试发帖，持续一两个月，观察效果再调整策略。（01:15:06）不过确实，我们合作过的很多高管都觉得这很难，他们会过度思考，追求完美，陷入自我纠结。我完全理解这种感受，因为我自己也一样。所以如果光是思考社交策略就占据了你大量时间和精力，那你可以评估一下是否值得继续，但我认为至少应该尝试一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then Aaron specifically is very good at this, is there anything that you learned from his approach to tweeting specifically? I don't know if he uses other platforms. That works really well for him.
turns.zh: 然后亚伦在这方面做得很棒。你从他的推特策略中学到了什么吗？我不知道他是否还用其他平台，但他的方法对他效果很好。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I actually think I just learned so much. So it was my first in-house job, so I had worked in an agency, I hadn't worked internally at a company before, and I think I just learned so much about comms best practices from him in general, just even beyond social. He was so good at figuring out how to comment on things happening in the news, having just the right stance that was both interesting to the reporter but not necessarily threatening to the business, and just capitalizing on all those moments. And I just watched how that worked and I was like, "This is how good PR is." And it's like the space that they're in is not necessarily one that reporters are all writing about, but he was able to insert himself in those conversations really well. And I think also at the time that I was there at least just really valued press and was willing to put the time in and do the briefings. (01:16:34): And so just getting to hear how he speaks over and over again was really helpful. And then on Twitter, I think it clearly just comes naturally to him, and so it wasn't necessarily something that needed to... Like I mentioned, how some execs will spend all this time thinking through to the point where it could get in the way of other things. I think that's not the case there. And if anything, it just helped the business. And actually with his Twitter presence, I would say it's a good example too of stuff getting included in articles, like I mentioned in that Microsoft article. So it helps the PR strategy as well.
turns.zh: 实际上，我觉得自己学到了很多东西。这是我第一份公司内部的工作，以前我在广告公司工作，从未在企业内部任职。我认为我从他那里学到了很多公关最佳实践，甚至不止是社交媒体方面。他非常善于把握新闻热点事件的评论时机，既能引起记者的兴趣，又不损害企业的利益，还能巧妙利用这些机会。我观察他是如何做到这一点的，心想：“这才是优秀的公关手段。” 他们的业务领域未必是记者们热衷报道的领域，但他能很好地融入这些对话。我记得当时我在那里，至少非常重视媒体关系，愿意投入时间做简报。（01:16:34）反复聆听他讲话真的很有帮助。在推特方面，我觉得这对他来说是自然而然的事情，不需要刻意准备。就像我提到的，有些高管会花大量时间深思熟虑，以至于影响其他工作。Aaron显然不是这样。相反，这对业务有帮助。实际上，就他的推特影响力而言，这也是一个很好的例子，比如我提到的微软那篇文章。它对公关策略也很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And we'll link to his Twitter account. This is Aaron, CEO of Box, by the way. I think I mentioned at the beginning and then we just started talking about Aaron. Also, I realize, he tweets about this sometimes, he actually makes money from Twitter, and now the Twitter pays you for views and things and they share ads, he makes thousands of dollars also from X now, by the way, not Twitter.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会附上他的推特账号。顺便说一句，Aaron是Box公司的首席执行官。我记得我一开始提到了他，然后我们就开始聊他了。还有，我发现他有时会在推特上分享这些内容，他确实能从推特赚钱。现在推特会根据阅读量付费，还会分享广告，他现在通过X平台也能赚不少钱，不过不是推特平台。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: That's so funny.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's pretty ridiculous. I think I've gone through every question that I had for you. I'm curious if there's anything else that you think might be helpful to share or cover or leave listeners with.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太荒谬了。我想我已经把想问你的问题都问完了。我很好奇是否还有其他有用的信息可以分享、探讨或者留给听众。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I can leave with one very tactical media opportunity that I love.
turns.zh: 我可以留一个我很喜欢的非常实用的媒体机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Okay, so here it is. It's a way to get a morning brew feature pretty somewhat easily. So they have this series called Morning Brew Coworking series, and they have it for Emerging Tech Brew, they have it for HR Brew, all their verticals. I think there's a CFO one, marketing one. And essentially if you go to the series, the coworking series, either at the top or the bottom, there's something where it's like, "If you want to be featured, click on this link and fill out this form," and it's about 10 questions. If you keep your answers interesting and fun and not too self-promotional, we've had, I would say, 50% success rate with getting execs featured that way. And all you have to do is submit through a Google form. And it's just one of my favorite media opportunities right now. It doesn't need to be CEO, actually probably shouldn't be a CEO in a lot of instances, but it's basically intended to help readers understand what the day-to-day looks in certain jobs and just get a little insight into the people that are in these jobs. And so I guess I just wanted to share that as something that you could do today for over 10 minutes and potentially get a story. Although, maybe not after you post this, so we'll see if they get an influx.
turns.zh: 好的，我现在要讲一下这个方法。想在Morning Brew上获得晨间专访的机会其实挺简单的。他们有系列专题，比如“新兴科技专访”、“人力资源专访”，以及其他垂直领域的专访。我记得还有CFO专访和市场营销专访。基本上如果你去浏览这些专访系列，无论是顶部还是底部，都会有一个提示：“如果想获得专访机会，请点击此链接并填写问卷”，问卷大约有10个问题。只要回答得有趣、生动且不过分自我推销，我们通过这种方式获得高管专访的成功率能达到50%。只需通过Google表单提交申请即可。这是我目前最喜欢的媒体推广机会之一。不过不一定非得是CEO，实际上很多情况下CEO可能不太适合参与，但这个专题主要是帮助读者了解某些职位的日常工作内容，深入了解这些职位从业者的真实生活。今天花10多分钟时间参与这个活动，可能就能获得专访机会。不过可能等你发布这段内容后效果就不太明显了，看看他们是否会迎来大量申请吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to take down Mailbrew. Funny enough, they have an interview with Zuck today that they published on Morning Brew, so it could be you alongside Zuck.
turns.zh: 我们要关闭Mailbrew了。有趣的是，他们今天在Morning Brew上发布了对扎克伯格的采访，万一你能和扎克伯格同框登场呢。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: There you go, yeah.
turns.zh: 就是这样，嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe before we get to our very exciting lightning round, it might be fun to chat about how to pick a PR agency. Obviously you run one. When people are trying to decide who to work with and also when to decide to pick and work with a PR agency versus doing it themselves, what advice can you share when they're trying to make that big decision?
turns.zh: 在我们开始激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，或许可以聊聊如何选择公关公司。显然你自己就经营着一家公关公司。当人们在决定与哪家公关公司合作时，或者在选择自己操作公关工作时，面对这个重大决策时，你能给出什么建议呢？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I think there's an assumption that bigger, more well-known agencies are going to do a better job. I think a lot of those bigger, well-known agencies are used to working with a lot of household brands. And so their strategies tend to be very reactive, focus in the messaging, maybe have to turn down a bunch of opportunities, control what people say. That is the polar opposite in my opinion of doing startup PR. Startup PR, you got to experiment, you got to try new things, you got to be scrappy, you got to be fast. We actually personally love diving into pitching right away rather than spending several months on messaging just testing and market right away. And so don't assume just because they have the huge logos... To your point, you're like, "Oh, well, you work with [inaudible 01:20:16] Perplexity, does that mean you know how to work with all these tiny companies?" (01:20:19): That's not necessarily a good thing, so don't just go buy the big logos. I would say that's my first piece of advice. My second piece of advice is find out what month one looks like with them. If month one is them just doing intake calls and learning about the company, and you're a startup that's still really paying close attention to how much money you're spending, you're not going to necessarily want to partner with an agency that needs a three-month ramp up cycle. And so really tactically understand what those first few months look like. I think that's something that I've noticed is a lot of agencies take a while before they get their hands dirty and start doing things. My third piece of advice would be writing recent writing samples. To the point of all those press release excerpts I shared, is that how they write? If it is, maybe they're not the right agency. So ask them. That's so easy. That's so easy to do. (01:21:14): Just ask them for a couple recent blogs or releases, whatever they tend to go for, and read those. And, of course, wins too. You want to see what kind of stories they're getting, but that's a little more obvious. A lot of people have already talked about this, so I'll just mention briefly, it's important to meet with the actual team you're working on, not just the founder of the agency. So asking who's our day-to-day going to be? Can we chat with them really quick? One thing I would say don't do is an extensive RFP process. We actually as an agency don't participate in RFPs. The two times I've done it, I have regretted it just because of the amount of work going in versus the value that's there. And it's you're asking a team to do a lot of free work for you, and generally I think the best players are not going to do that, so you're going to weed out some of the best players if you're asking them to do a lot of free upfront work. So those are a few considerations.
turns.zh:
我认为人们往往会默认大型知名公关公司能提供更优质的服务。但实际上，这些大牌机构大多习惯与大品牌合作，因此他们的策略往往比较被动——专注于信息传递，可能需要拒绝大量合作机会，并试图控制舆论导向。这与初创企业公关的理念截然相反。初创企业公关需要勇于尝试新事物，保持灵活高效。我们个人更倾向于立即开展宣传推广，而不是花数月时间打磨信息再推向市场。  

别以为那些挂着大牌Logo的公司就一定专业。（01:20:19）你可能会问：“哦，他们和Perplexity合作过，这是否意味着他们能处理所有小型公司的公关需求？”这未必是件好事，所以别被华丽的外表蒙蔽了。我的首要建议是：先了解他们的服务流程。若第一个月只是进行项目接洽和了解公司情况，而你所在的初创企业还需要严格控制预算，那显然不适合与需要三个月准备期的公关公司合作。务必深入了解前几个月的具体服务内容。  

我发现许多公关公司需要很久才能真正投入工作。这里有个简单方法：查看他们近期的媒体稿样本。若文案风格千篇一律，那可能不适合你。所以直接问他们：能否分享近期博客或新闻稿，特别是那些成功案例？这样能直观评估他们的专业水平。  

（01:21:14）还要注意获奖案例。当然，获奖案例更直观，但许多人已谈及此处，我只简要补充一点：务必与实际负责团队会面，而非仅与创始人沟通。例如：“我们的日常沟通对象是谁？能快速与他们交流吗？”  

最后，别陷入冗长的RFP流程。我们公司从不参与RFP投标。仅参与过两次，都后悔不已，因为投入精力与实际价值不成正比。这等于让团队免费为你打工，而优秀的团队通常不愿这样。所以，别让过多前期免费工作筛选掉最优秀的合作伙伴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. And then just two more questions, because I imagine this is what people are thinking about when they're trying to decide should we find somebody is how long ahead of time they should find someone before something big is happening? And then just what's a budget they should have in mind for something like this? What's a minimum or a range, whatever you think would be helpful for people to understand here's how much you're probably going to be investing here?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那再问两个问题吧，因为我猜人们在决定是否要找人帮忙时，最关心的可能是：在重大活动来临前多久才应该开始寻找合适的人选呢？然后就是预算方面，针对这种情况，他们应该预留多少资金呢？最低预算是多少？或者说一个合理的预算范围是怎样的？您觉得这些信息对人们理解投资成本会有帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Start times can vary from agency to agency. I think we can get started the week that a client needs us to, so maybe I'm not best equipped to answer this, but I would say before an announcement happens, you probably want to kick off six weeks in advance. So when we start with the company, it's like we're working on the blog, we're doing a media training, we're doing the media outreach, we're getting quotes from investors, or coordinating with all the parties, making sure images are being created so it's not just pitching and securing the article. So I would say buffer with time to pitch, make sure that the reporter is actually able to cover it. Six weeks is ideal. I would also note I highly recommend not having a firm date that you think you need to announce something and going instead with when a reporter is able to cover your story. (01:23:12): We get so many clients that come to us and they have this set date in their head, but there's not usually a real reason for it. It's like they're planning around it, it's like they have other comms they want to go out that day, but if you can optimize for the reporter over the timing, you're going to see such a better outcome because getting the first choice reporter is going to drive way more for your business than announcing it four days sooner. So leaving a little bit of flexibility for that agency is key. And I've even seen companies like issue a press release for big news with no coverage because they had stuck to a certain day and were very rigid about it, and they didn't get any stories for that reason. And so I think a good agency would counsel to offer that flexibility. (01:23:54): So six weeks I think is the ideal amount of time. And then budget, I would say the lowest end would probably be about 10K a month for an agency. You can find consultants, I think the best ones would be at least 8K a month, but for a small boutique agency starts at 10. I'll just be transparent, I'm very open about our pricing, our rates start at 15K a month for our retainers, and actually that's for a series A companies generally what they're at. And then I would say unless you are a global business that needs basically different teams for different product lines, which happens when you're a Microsoft of the world, that's another story. But if you're just a series C startup that's getting a lot of attention, I wouldn't go beyond 30K probably. There are plenty of agencies that go into the 50s and 60s a month, but that's just a whole nother world, and I'm not an expert on that part.
turns.zh: 不同公关公司的启动时间各不相同。我觉得我们可以根据客户的需求随时开始工作，所以或许我没法给出一个准确的答案。但我建议，在正式宣布之前，至少要提前六周开始筹备。比如，我们会和客户一起筹备博客内容、开展媒体培训、联系媒体、收集投资者的引语，或者协调各方事宜，确保图片素材到位，这样不仅仅是推销和争取稿件的机会。所以我认为要预留足够的时间用于推销，确保记者能有效报道你的新闻。六周的时间是最理想的。另外，我强烈建议不要执着于一个固定的宣布日期，而应根据记者的报道周期来安排。（01:23:12）：很多客户来找我们时，他们脑子里已经有了一个固定日期，但通常这并没有实际意义。他们可能只是根据这个日期来规划其他公关活动，但如果你能根据记者的报道周期来调整时间安排，效果会好得多。因为获得首选记者的报道机会，对你的业务价值远超提前四天宣布。所以给公关公司留出灵活调整的时间至关重要。我甚至见过一些公司因为执着于某个固定日期、过于僵化，导致新闻稿发布后无人报道的情况。所以我认为一个好的公关公司应该建议客户根据实际情况调整时间。（01:23:54）：所以六周的时间是最理想的。至于预算，我觉得最低标准可能是每月1万美元。对于公关公司来说，8千美元可能更合适，但小型精品公司起步价是1万美元。我会很坦诚地说，我们的定价起步是每月1.5万美元，这基本符合A轮融资公司的标准。除非你是像微软这样的全球性企业，需要为不同产品线配备不同团队，那就是另一回事了。但如果你只是一个备受关注的C轮初创公司，预算应该不超过3万美元。当然，也有许多公关公司收费达到5万到6万美元，但那就是另一个层级了，我对此不算专家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Thank you for sharing all that. What if you're going for just a one-off, just help me get one story, what's a range there for budget you should expect?
turns.zh: 太棒了。感谢你分享这些信息。如果我只需要一次性的服务，比如帮我拿下一个报道，你预计预算范围是多少？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I would say between 10 and 20. And you might be able to find a consultant that'll do it for eight.
turns.zh: 我觉得在1万到2万美元之间。可能你能找到8千美元就能完成的顾问。

turns.en: Amazing. So helpful. Emilie, is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?

turns.en: No. I'm ready.
turns.zh: 没有了。我准备好了。

turns.en: I am.

turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.en: And ever since researching that field, there's the whole concept of changing your neural pathways is just very fascinating to me. And so I'm really excited about it.
turns.zh: 自从研究这个领域以来，改变神经通路的整个概念对我来说非常着迷。开放思维、转换视角对我来说非常重要，即使是在经营公司、成为更好的领导者方面。我认为我们目前正处于一个快速发展的阶段，招聘大量员工，压力很大，我只想确保每天都能展现出最好的自己。所以我对此非常兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an amazing answer. This is going to be part of your set and setting this interview, but hopefully you can get it out of your mind.
turns.zh: 真是个很棒的回答。这将成为你这次采访的一部分，但希望你能暂时忘掉这些。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: No, totally. I was nervous. I'm like, "It's actually really great that this is happening and then I can completely unplug after it. And so I think it's actually good timing.
turns.zh: 不，完全没关系。我很紧张。我在想，“这真的很棒，能有这样的经历，之后我就能彻底放松了。所以我觉得这时机正好。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to hear how it goes.
turns.zh: 我很期待听到结果如何。

turns.en: I'm not a big book recommender. I have ADHD and reading full books is very hard for me, and so I'm just going to leave you with that one. I can do the occasional beach read I'll really focus, but it's not my main format of content consumption.
turns.zh: 我不太擅长推荐书籍。我有注意力缺失症，读完整本书对我来说很难。所以我就只推荐一本吧。我偶尔会读些海滩读物，集中精力，但这不是我主要的阅读方式。

turns.en: Amazing. All right, great answer. One's plenty. Do you have a favorite movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，回答得很棒。一个就够了。你有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.en: My favorite genre is post-apocalyptic, end of the world survival. I need to mention my all time favorite show, because it would be bad not to. turns.zh: 我最喜欢的类型是末日题材、世界末日求生题材。我必须提到我最喜欢的剧集，不然就太失礼了。所以《行尸走肉》是我最喜欢的舒适剧，晚上睡觉时可以看，但我最近最喜欢的剧是《黄蜂队》。你们听说过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've seen the poster on my TV, but I've not watched it.
turns.zh: 我在电视上看到过这部剧的宣传片，但还没看过。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Nice. I discovered it a little late. I think the second season finished and they're working on the third. But it has plane crash, and it has just shocking moment after shocking moment like cannibalism, very weird stuff. turns.zh: 不错。我发现得有点晚了。我想第二季已经结束了，他们正在筹备第三季。不过里面有飞机失事的情节，还有一个接一个令人震惊的场景，比如吃人肉之类的，非常离奇。这部剧会让你印象深刻，我喜欢那种看完后还回味许久的感觉。确实有点令人毛骨悚然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I thought you were going for Last of Us, but I now have to watch this show.
turns.zh: 哇。我还以为你说的是《最后生还者》呢，不过现在我得去看看这部剧了。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: No, I watched Last of Us and I didn't feel like it had enough survival elements to it. It was like storytelling in that environment, but it wasn't actually a survival post-apocalyptic show in the way that I was looking for.
turns.zh: 不，我看过《最后生还者》，但觉得它没有足够的生存元素。它更像是在那种环境下讲故事，但并没有真正符合我所期待的末日生存题材。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hardcore. Do you have a favorite interview question you like to ask? And you could take this in any direction you want.
turns.zh: 太难了。你有没有最喜欢问的采访问题？而且你可以随意发挥这个方向。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah. I have a new one. We actually just revamped our interview process, so I wanted to make it harder. So my new favorite question is if a client comes to you and they're convinced they have something that's press worthy, like an announcement that they think should be, I don't know, in the Wall Street Journal or something, and you know for a fact that it isn't, what steps do you take? What do you do next? And I like that question because they can handle it, one, from the client relations standpoint, how do you communicate with the client when they say something like that, but it's also a critical thinking and creativity question of how do you take a no and turn it into a yes? How do you take what they're giving you and make it into something interesting? And so I like to dig into that, and they can use a real example if they want, but I also think a lot of our job is pushing back in a way. And so that also shows if they're able and willing to push back.
turns.zh: 有啊。我刚想出一个新问题。我们最近优化了采访流程，所以想把难度提高一点。我现在最喜欢的问题是，如果客户来找你，坚信自己有值得媒体报道的新闻，比如他们认为应该登上《华尔街日报》之类的头条，而你明明知道这根本不可能，你会采取什么步骤？接下来该怎么做？我喜欢这个问题，因为它既能考验客户关系处理能力，又能测试批判性思维和创造力——如何把否定转化为肯定？如何把客户提供的素材变成有趣的内容？所以我喜欢深入探讨这个问题，如果他们愿意，还可以举实际案例，但我觉得我们的工作很大程度上就是要反驳客户的想法。这也能看出他们是否有能力和意愿去反驳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so curious to hear people's answer to that. Do you have a favorite product that you recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 我很想听听大家对这个问题的回答。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.en: I was very skeptical of Apple Vision Pro and I was making fun of it at the beginning, and the first time I tried it, I completely changed my tune, I'm so into it, I'm ordering one, and I'm very excited for actually using it for work. I'm like, "Do we have an Apple Vision Pro strategy? Are we billing to talk about it publicly yet?" Because sometimes it's tying back to the PR conversation, I love if you're willing to push the envelope on stuff that you are building or are going to do and getting ahead of those conversations, so that's a lot of conversations I'm having right now is trying to convince clients to talk about that.
turns.zh: 我一开始对Apple Vision Pro持怀疑态度，甚至还拿它开玩笑。但当我第一次试用后，态度完全转变了。我现在超爱它，已经下单购买，而且特别期待能在工作中实际使用它。我觉得它对我的日常工作来说是个非常棒的应用场景。试用结束后，第二天我就给一群可能对它有相关应用需求的客户发消息。我问：“我们有Apple Vision Pro的战略吗？我们有没有公开谈论它的计划？”因为有时候这会涉及到公关策略。我希望大家能大胆尝试正在开发或即将推出的项目，抢占先机。现在我正花大量时间说服客户参与相关讨论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you have an Apple Vision Pro strategy, amazing.
turns.zh: 所以你们已经有Apple Vision Pro的战略了，太棒了。

turns.en: And then my other one, which is very self-serving, because they are a client, but I do use them every day, is Perplexity. Or writing a bio for an executive, getting just the TLDR of what they've done in their past, it's so good for PR use cases, and I actually think marketing and PR is going to be one of the core work applications for them.
turns.zh: 还有另一个我用得超多的产品，虽然它是客户的服务，但我每天都会用，那就是Perplexity。它对我帮助很大。比如我在准备奖项申请时，忘记了客户筹集了多少资金，直接问他们，比起打开五个不同的谷歌链接去查找答案，Perplexity能快速获取信息，真是太棒了。或者给高管写简介时，能快速了解他们过往的成就，这对公关场景非常有用。我甚至认为营销和公关将成为Perplexity的核心应用场景之一。

turns.en: I've also already shared how much I love Perplexity, I have the Chrome extension installed. I probably use it at least once a day for podcast interview prep along with a bunch of other stuff. So good find for customer. I think they're going to do great. Wish I was an investor.
turns.zh: 我已经跟别人分享过我对Perplexity的热爱了，我安装了Chrome扩展程序。每天至少用一次来准备播客采访，还有其他各种用途。对客户来说真是宝藏产品。我觉得他们会大获成功的。真希望我也是投资者。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: I'm the happy investor. I rarely angel invest and I was...

turns.zh: 好的，还有两个问题。你有没有一个最喜欢的的人生格言，经常回味、与朋友或家人分享，无论是在工作中还是生活中？

turns.en: Emilie, this was everything I hoped it would be. I feel like this is going to help so many people get awesome press. Thank you again so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you and reach out if they want to learn more or work with you? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 埃米莉，这次访谈完全超出了我的预期。我觉得这将帮助很多人，让他们获得绝佳的宣传机会。再次感谢你能来参加访谈。最后两个问题：如果人们想了解更多信息或与你合作，可以在哪里找到你？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Our website is sixeastern.com and our email is hello@sixeastern.com, so you can find us there. And actually I have a newsletter called On Background. It's on Substack. And really what it's intended to be is a place for people to find these tactical opportunities, so it has media moves, it has reporters that are working on stories, it has awards that are open, all of this stuff that basically an intern in an agency would spend their days researching we put into a newsletter. And so its main audience is PR people, but I actually think it could be a great resource for people within companies that don't have PR teams to stay on top of stuff. So I guess to be helpful, feel free to subscribe. And then other than that, we're hiring, so if you happen to be a PR person that got this far in the episode, always looking for great people to bring on.
turns.zh: 我们的网站是sixeastern.com，邮箱是hello@sixeastern.com，大家可以在那里找到我们。实际上，我还有一个名为On Background的时事通讯，发布在Substack上。这个平台旨在为人们提供战术性机遇的信息，包括媒体动态、正在报道新闻的记者、开放的奖项等——这些都是实习生每天需要查找的信息，我们把这些内容整合成时事通讯。因此，它的主要读者是公关从业者，但我认为对于没有公关团队的公司员工来说，这也是一个很好的资源。所以如果大家觉得有用，随时可以订阅。此外，我们正在招聘，如果有听众对公关工作感兴趣，欢迎联系我们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Is there anything specific you're looking for in people you're hiring for people that may want to reach out other than they've been in PR?
turns.zh: 太棒了。对于应聘者，你有没有特别的要求？除了具备公关经验之外，还需要其他条件吗？

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Ideally some B2B experience. I think doing B2B PR is very different from doing consumer PR. If you work with startups, that's a huge plus, you know how to be kind of scrappy and fast. And also people that just love to be really hands-on and doing the actual work. We're very flat, so we're not a place where there's much managing of teams. So it's really much more like a consultancy than anything else.
turns.zh: 理想情况下，应聘者应有B2B领域的经验。我认为B2B公关与面向消费者的公关有很大不同。如果应聘者有创业公司工作经验，那就更理想了，因为他们更善于灵活应变、快速行动。同时，我们希望应聘者乐于亲力亲为，参与实际工作。我们公司结构扁平，没有太多层级管理，所以这里更像是一家咨询公司而非传统公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Emilie, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。埃米莉，非常感谢你能来参加访谈。

turns.speaker: Emilie Gerber
turns.en: Yeah, it was so fun. Thank you so much.
turns.zh: 是啊，这次访谈太有趣了。非常感谢。
